4-1.bio:
St. Mary of Egypt is the great example of repentance. Living in Alexandria in the fifth and sixth centuries, she spent her youth in sin; traveling to Jerusalem, she was held back from entering the Church of the Holy Sepulchre by an unseen power, and, praying before the icon of the Theotokos, she was converted. Crossing the Jordan, she lived some forty-seven years alone in the desert in fasting and prayer.

Near the end of her life she was found by the elder Zosimas, who heard her story and gave her Holy Communion. She is commemorated on April 1 and on the fifth Sunday of Great Lent.
4-1.desc: Venerable Mary of Egypt, great penitent saint.
4-1.name: Mary of Egypt

4-1.bio:
Makarios was born in Constantinople and, orphaned young, was raised by a pious uncle who gave him a thorough grounding in Scripture. He entered the Monastery of Pelekete in Bithynia and in time became its abbot, known for his humility and gift of healing.

When the iconoclast emperors renewed their persecution of icon-venerators, Makarios refused to renounce the holy images and was imprisoned and exiled. Tradition relates that he died in exile in the ninth century, faithful to the end.
4-1.desc: Venerable Makarios the Confessor, abbot of the Pelekete Monastery in Bithynia, who suffered exile for the holy icons.
4-1.name: Makarios of Pelekete

4-1.bio:
Gerontios and Basilides are commemorated together as martyrs of the early centuries of the Church. The synaxaria record that they confessed Christ before the pagan authorities and were beheaded by the sword.

Little else is preserved of their lives, but the Church has kept their names among the confessors whose blood watered the seed of the faith.
4-1.desc: Holy Martyrs Gerontios and Basilides, who were beheaded for their confession of Christ.
4-1.name: Gerontios and Basilides

4-1.bio:
Hermes and Theodora were siblings who confessed the Christian faith together and were put to death for it. The Greek synaxaria list them among the martyrs commemorated on the first of April.

Tradition relates only that they endured their martyrdom side by side, encouraging one another until the end.
4-1.desc: Holy Martyrs Hermes and Theodora, brother and sister, who suffered together for Christ.
4-1.name: Hermes and Theodora

4-1.bio:
Abraham was a wealthy merchant of the Volga Bulgars, raised in Islam, who came to believe in Christ and was baptized. He became known for his generosity to the poor and for his open confession of the Christian faith among his countrymen.

Tradition relates that when he refused to return to his former religion he was tortured and beheaded in the thirteenth century. His relics were later carried to the city of Vladimir, where he has been venerated as a wonderworker.
4-1.desc: Holy New Martyr Abraham of Bulgaria, a Volga merchant who embraced Christ and was killed by his own people.
4-1.name: Abraham of Bulgaria

4-1.bio:
Euthymius was born in Nizhny Novgorod in the fourteenth century and received his monastic formation under Saint Dionysius of the Caves monastery there. At the invitation of the prince of Suzdal he founded the Monastery of the Saviour in that city and governed it as archimandrite for many years.

He was a friend and contemporary of Saint Sergius of Radonezh and was known for strict asceticism and care for the poor. He reposed in peace and his relics were later uncovered incorrupt.
4-1.desc: Venerable Euthymius, archimandrite and founder of the Saviour Monastery in Suzdal.
4-1.name: Euthymius of Suzdal

4-1.bio:
Barsanuphius, born Paul Plikhankov in 1845, served as an officer in the Russian army before leaving a promising career to enter the Optina Hermitage in middle age. He became a disciple of the elder Anatole and was in time made skete superior and spiritual father to many.

During the Russo-Japanese War he served as a military chaplain. He was later transferred from Optina and reposed in 1913 at the Golutvin Monastery. He is numbered among the holy Optina Elders.
4-1.desc: Venerable Barsanuphius, elder of the Optina Hermitage and former army officer.
4-1.name: Barsanuphius of Optina

4-10.bio:
St. Terence was a martyr of North Africa who suffered in the third century, during the persecution of the emperor Decius. Together with a company of fellow Christians, he confessed Christ before the proconsul, endured imprisonment and torments without wavering, and was beheaded with his companions.

The Church remembers this band of African martyrs as an image of brotherly steadfastness, many suffering as one body for the one Lord. St. Terence and his companions are commemorated on April 10.
4-10.name: Terence

4-10.bio:
Gregory was born in Dimitsana in the Peloponnese in the eighteenth century and rose to become Metropolitan of Smyrna and three times Ecumenical Patriarch. He was known for his austerity, his charity, and his care for the education of his people.

When the Greek revolution broke out in 1821, the Ottomans seized him on Easter Sunday and hanged him from the gate of the Patriarchate, which has remained shut ever since. His relics rest in the Cathedral of Athens.
4-10.desc: Hieromartyr Gregory V, Patriarch of Constantinople, hanged at the gate of the Patriarchate in 1821.
4-10.name: Gregory V of Constantinople

4-10.bio:
Huldah was a prophetess in Jerusalem in the reign of King Josiah. When the Book of the Law was found in the Temple, the king sent to her, and she declared the word of the Lord concerning the coming judgment on Judah and the peace granted to Josiah for his humility.

Her story is told in the Second Book of Kings and the Second Book of Chronicles.
4-10.desc: Holy Prophetess Huldah, who spoke the word of the Lord in the days of King Josiah.
4-10.name: Huldah the Prophetess

4-10.bio:
James, a priest, and Azas, a deacon, were arrested in Persia during the persecution of King Shapur in the fourth century. They endured severe torture for refusing to worship the sun.

They were put to death for Christ and are honoured with the other martyrs of Persia.
4-10.desc: Holy Martyrs James the Presbyter and Azas the Deacon of Persia.
4-10.greek: Ιάκωβος ο Πρεσβύτερος και Αζάς ο Διάκονος
4-10.name: James the Presbyter and Azas the Deacon

4-10.bio:
Demos was a fisherman from Adrianople who worked in Smyrna. Tradition relates that a Turkish employer, angered by a dispute, accused him falsely of having promised to embrace Islam.

Brought before the judge, he confessed Christ and refused every inducement, and was beheaded at Smyrna in the eighteenth century.
4-10.desc: Holy New Martyr Demos the Fisherman of Adrianople, martyred at Smyrna.
4-10.name: Demos the Fisherman

4-10.bio:
Chrysanthos was a monk of the Monastery of Xenophontos on Mount Athos. Tradition relates that he went to Constantinople and there openly confessed Christ before the Ottoman authorities.

He was put to death for his confession in the years of Ottoman rule and is honoured among the Athonite new martyrs.
4-10.desc: Holy New Martyr Chrysanthos, monk of the Xenophontos Monastery on Mount Athos.
4-10.name: Chrysanthos of Xenophontos

4-10.bio:
Miltiades was Bishop of Rome in the early fourth century, in the years when the persecutions ended and the emperor Constantine granted freedom to the Church. He presided over a synod at Rome that examined the Donatist dispute in Africa.

He reposed in peace and is remembered as one of the last popes of the age of the martyrs.
4-10.desc: Saint Miltiades, Pope of Rome in the days of the emperor Constantine.
4-10.name: Miltiades of Rome

4-11.bio:
St. Antipas was Bishop of Pergamon in Asia Minor in the first century, a disciple of the Apostle John. He is named in the Book of Revelation, where the Lord Himself calls him my faithful witness, slain among you where Satan dwells. Tradition relates that he was put to death by the pagans of Pergamon for refusing to honor their idols.

From ancient times the faithful have sought his intercession, invoking him especially for relief from ailments of the teeth. He is commemorated on April 11.
4-11.name: Antipas of Pergamon

4-11.bio:
Tryphaena and Matrona are listed together in the Greek synaxaria as venerable women who reposed in peace. Little has been preserved of their lives beyond their names and the memory of their holiness.

They are distinct from the martyr Tryphaena of Cyzicus and from the venerable Matrona of Constantinople, who are commemorated on other days.
4-11.desc: Venerable Tryphaena and Matrona, holy women commemorated together in the Greek synaxaria.
4-11.name: Tryphaena and Matrona

4-11.bio:
Pharmuthios lived as an anchorite in the Egyptian desert in the fourth century. Tradition relates that he was the elder who brought bread, miraculously supplied, to the hermit John who lived in a dry well.

He reposed in peace in the desert.
4-11.desc: Venerable Pharmuthios, anchorite of Egypt, who fed Saint John of the Well.
4-11.name: Pharmuthios the Anchorite

4-11.bio:
George was a Cypriot ascetic of the eleventh century who founded the Monastery of Saint John Chrysostom on the slopes of the Pentadaktylos range near Koutsovendis. He gathered a community there and guided it in the monastic life.

He reposed in peace and is venerated among the saints of Cyprus.
4-11.desc: Venerable George, founder of the Monastery of Saint John Chrysostom at Koutsovendis in Cyprus.
4-11.name: George of the Chrysostom Monastery

4-11.bio:
Barsanuphius was born in Serpukhov in the fifteenth century and as a youth was captured by the Crimean Tatars, among whom he learned their language while remaining steadfast in the faith. Ransomed by his father, he became a monk.

After the conquest of Kazan he founded the Transfiguration Monastery there and preached to the Tatars in their own tongue. He was later made Bishop of Tver and reposed in the sixteenth century, returning to Kazan in his last years.
4-11.desc: Saint Barsanuphius, Bishop of Tver, former captive of the Tatars and founder of a monastery in Kazan.
4-11.name: Barsanuphius of Tver

4-11.bio:
Callinicus was born in Bucharest in 1787 and became a monk at the Cernica Monastery, whose abbot he was for many years, renowned for fasting, prayer and charity. He was later made Bishop of Ramnic, where he rebuilt churches and founded schools.

He returned to Cernica at the end of his life and reposed in 1868. He is one of the most beloved saints of the Romanian Church.
4-11.desc: Saint Callinicus of Cernica, Bishop of Ramnic, ascetic and builder of churches in Romania.
4-11.name: Callinicus of Cernica

4-11.bio:
Processus and Martinian were, according to tradition, guards of the Mamertine prison in Rome who came to faith through the preaching of the Apostles Peter and Paul, whom they held in custody. They were baptized by the apostles.

For this they themselves were arrested and beheaded in the persecution of Nero.
4-11.desc: Holy Martyrs Processus and Martinian, jailers of Rome converted by the Apostles Peter and Paul.
4-11.name: Processus and Martinian

4-12.bio:
St. Basil was Bishop of Parion in Asia Minor during the age of iconoclasm. Refusing to consent to the condemnation of the holy icons, he was driven from his see and spent long years in hardship and wandering, enduring persecution rather than betray the fullness of the faith.

The Church numbers him among the confessors whose sufferings preserved the veneration of the icons for the whole Orthodox world. He is commemorated on April 12.
4-12.name: Basil of Parion

4-12.bio:
Anthusa was the daughter of the iconoclast emperor Constantine V and twin sister of the future emperor Leo. Unlike her father she loved the holy icons and refused every proposal of marriage, giving her wealth to the poor.

After her father's death she became a nun in a convent she founded in Constantinople, and reposed in peace in the early ninth century.
4-12.desc: Venerable Anthusa, daughter of the iconoclast emperor Constantine Copronymus, who became a nun.
4-12.name: Anthusa of Constantinople

4-12.bio:
Artemon served the Church of Laodicea in Syria first as reader and then as deacon and presbyter for many years. In the persecution of Diocletian he was arrested and, tradition relates, worked wonders that led many to faith.

He was beheaded at the beginning of the fourth century.
4-12.desc: Hieromartyr Artemon, presbyter of Laodicea, who suffered under Diocletian.
4-12.name: Artemon of Laodicea

4-12.bio:
Akakios was born in the Agrapha mountains in the seventeenth century and became a monk on Mount Athos, settling finally in the cave of Saint Maximus at Kavsokalyvia. There he lived in extreme asceticism and was granted gifts of prayer and foresight.

He prepared and blessed several monks who went out to martyrdom for Christ under the Ottomans. He reposed at a great age in 1730.
4-12.desc: Venerable Akakios the Younger of Kavsokalyvia on Mount Athos, guide of new martyrs.
4-12.name: Akakios of Kavsokalyvia

4-12.bio:
Menas, David and John were monks of Palestine who were seized by Arab raiders in the seventh century. Refusing to deny Christ, they were shot with arrows.

They are honoured among the monastic martyrs of the Holy Land.
4-12.desc: Holy Monk-Martyrs Menas, David and John of Palestine, slain by arrows.
4-12.name: Menas, David and John

4-12.bio:
Neophytos was born in Cyprus in the twelfth century and, after years of monastic life, carved a cell for himself in a cliff near Paphos, the Enkleistra, where he lived in seclusion. Disciples gathered around him and a monastery grew up at the site.

He wrote many works of instruction and commentary and reposed in peace in the early thirteenth century. His relics are venerated at his monastery.
4-12.desc: Venerable Neophytos the Recluse of Cyprus, hermit and spiritual writer of the Enkleistra near Paphos.
4-12.name: Neophytos the Recluse

4-12.bio:
Sabbas was a Goth living in the lands north of the Danube who served as a reader in the Christian community there. When the Gothic chieftain Athanaric persecuted the Christians, Sabbas openly refused to eat food offered to idols and was arrested.

He was drowned in the river Buzau in 372, and the account of his martyrdom, written by the local Church, is one of the earliest records of Christianity in Romania.
4-12.desc: Holy Martyr Sabbas the Goth, drowned in the river Buzau in Wallachia.
4-12.name: Sabbas the Goth

4-13.bio:
St. Martin the Confessor was Pope of Rome in the seventh century. He convened a council at the Lateran which condemned the Monothelite heresy, defending the fullness of Christ's humanity against the will of the emperor. For this he was seized by imperial soldiers, carried off to Constantinople, tried and mistreated, and exiled to Cherson on the Black Sea.

Worn down by hunger and hardship, he died in exile, a confessor for the Orthodox faith honored by East and West alike. He is commemorated on April 13.
4-13.name: Martin the Confessor

4-13.bio:
Zoilos is commemorated in the Greek synaxaria as a martyr of Rome who gave his life for Christ. Little has been preserved of his story beyond his name and his witness.

He is one of the many martyrs of the early Church whose memory survives in the calendar alone.
4-13.name: Zoilos the Roman

4-13.bio:
Maximus, a reader of the Church, with his companions Quintilian and Dadas, were denounced as Christians at Ozovia near Dorostolum in Moesia during the persecution of Diocletian. They refused to sacrifice to the idols.

After imprisonment and torture they were beheaded at the end of the third century.
4-13.desc: Holy Martyrs Quintilian, Maximus the Reader and Dadas, beheaded near Dorostolum.
4-13.name: Quintilian, Maximus and Dadas

4-13.bio:
Eleutherios was a Christian of Persia who suffered for the faith in the persecutions of the Persian kings. The synaxaria record that he was put to death for confessing Christ.

He is distinct from the hieromartyr Eleutherios commemorated in December.
4-13.name: Eleutherios the Persian

4-13.bio:
Arsenios was born in Thessaly in the sixteenth century and became Archbishop of Elassona. Sent on Church business to Moscow, he remained in Russia, took part in the establishment of the Moscow Patriarchate, and was later made Archbishop of Suzdal.

He was a scholar and a builder of churches and reposed in Suzdal in 1625, where his relics are venerated.
4-13.desc: Saint Arsenios, Archbishop of Elassona and later Archbishop of Suzdal in Russia.
4-13.name: Arsenios of Elassona

4-14.bio:
St. Martin, Pope of Rome, was one of the great confessors of the seventh century. When the Monothelite heresy, supported by the imperial court, denied the fullness of Christ's human will, Martin gathered a council at the Lateran which condemned the error. The emperor's men seized the ailing pope, brought him in chains to Constantinople, and after a humiliating trial banished him to distant Cherson.

There, abandoned and deprived of necessities, he died for the faith he would not compromise. He is commemorated on April 14.
4-14.desc: Hieromartyr Martin the Confessor, Pope of Rome.
4-14.name: Martin the Confessor, Pope of Rome

4-14.bio:
Thomais was a young married woman of Alexandria in the fifth century, raised in piety. Her father-in-law, inflamed with passion, attempted to force her while her husband was away, and when she resisted he killed her with a sword.

She was buried with honour at a monastery near the city, and the fathers of the desert taught that those struggling with carnal temptation should seek her prayers.
4-14.desc: Holy Martyr Thomais of Alexandria, who died defending her chastity.
4-14.name: Thomais of Alexandria

4-14.bio:
Ardalion was a mime who, during a performance mocking the Christian martyrs, was suddenly moved by grace and declared before the theatre that he truly believed in Christ. The audience thought it part of the play until he repeated his confession in earnest.

He was burned alive in the persecution of the early fourth century.
4-14.desc: Holy Martyr Ardalion the Actor, who confessed Christ upon the stage.
4-14.name: Ardalion the Actor

4-14.bio:
Demetrios was born in the Peloponnese and as a boy, in the service of a Turkish master, was induced to accept Islam. Coming to himself, he repented bitterly and, after preparation on Mount Athos and elsewhere, returned to confess Christ openly before the judge at Tripolitsa.

He was beheaded there in 1803 and is honoured among the new martyrs of the Peloponnese.
4-14.desc: Holy New Martyr Demetrios the Peloponnesian, beheaded at Tripolitsa.
4-14.name: Demetrios the Peloponnesian

4-14.bio:
Anthony and John were brothers at the court of the Grand Duke of Lithuania who embraced Christianity and refused to observe pagan customs; their kinsman Eustathius followed them. All three were imprisoned and tortured for their faith.

They were hanged from an oak tree in Vilnius in the fourteenth century, and a monastery was later built on the site of their martyrdom.
4-14.desc: Holy Martyrs Anthony, John and Eustathius of Vilnius, hanged for Christ in pagan Lithuania.
4-14.name: Anthony, John and Eustathius of Vilnius

4-14.bio:
Christodoulos and Anastasia are honoured with a company of Christians who were put to death by the Turks in the Peloponnese at the outbreak of the Greek revolution in 1821, refusing to deny their faith.

They are numbered among the new martyrs of Achaia.
4-14.desc: Holy New Martyrs Christodoulos and Anastasia, and those with them, who suffered in the Peloponnese.
4-14.name: Christodoulos and Anastasia of Achaia

4-14.bio:
The Monastery of Daou on Mount Penteli near Athens was attacked by pirates who, tradition relates, slaughtered the entire brotherhood of one hundred and seventy-nine monks during the years of Ottoman rule.

Their bones were found in the monastery and are venerated there as relics of the martyrs.
4-14.desc: The Holy 179 Monk-Martyrs of the Monastery of Daou Penteli in Attica.
4-14.name: Monk-Martyrs of Daou Penteli

4-15.bio:
The holy Apostles Aristarchus, Pudens, and Trophimus were of the Seventy, fellow laborers of the Apostle Paul who are named in his epistles. Aristarchus shared Paul's journeys and imprisonment; Pudens received the faithful into his house in Rome; Trophimus accompanied Paul on his travels and shared his final trials.

According to tradition, all three completed their apostolic course as martyrs in Rome in the days of Nero, beheaded for the name of Christ. They are commemorated together on April 15.
4-15.desc: Holy Apostles of the Seventy: Aristarchus, Pudens, and Trophimus.
4-15.name: Apostles Aristarchus, Pudens & Trophimus

4-15.bio:
Leonides was Bishop of Athens in the third century. During the persecution of Decius he was arrested and taken to Corinth, where he was tried with seven Christian women who had been converted by his preaching.

After torture they were all cast into the sea, tradition relating that Leonides went to his death singing psalms. His memory is kept on this day in Athens, and on the following day with his companions of Corinth.
4-15.desc: Hieromartyr Leonides, Bishop of Athens, drowned at Corinth with the holy women who followed him.
4-15.name: Leonides of Athens

4-15.bio:
Crescens was a Christian of noble family in Myra of Lycia who openly urged the pagans of the city to abandon their idols and believe in Christ. He was arrested by the prefect and refused every demand to sacrifice.

He was burned alive and received the crown of martyrdom in the third century.
4-15.desc: Holy Martyr Crescens of Myra in Lycia, burned for Christ.
4-15.name: Crescens of Myra

4-15.bio:
Anastasia and Basilissa were noble women of Rome, disciples of the Apostles Peter and Paul. Tradition relates that after the apostles' martyrdom they recovered and buried their bodies.

For this they were denounced to the emperor Nero, tortured, and beheaded in the first century.
4-15.desc: Holy Martyrs Anastasia and Basilissa of Rome, who buried the bodies of the Apostles Peter and Paul.
4-15.name: Anastasia and Basilissa of Rome

4-15.bio:
Ananias Lampardis was Metropolitan of Lacedaemon in the Peloponnese in the eighteenth century, a hierarch of learning who cared for the education and welfare of his flock under Ottoman rule.

Accused of stirring his people against the Turks, he was seized and beheaded in 1767, and is honoured as a hieromartyr of the Church of Greece.
4-15.desc: Hieromartyr Ananias, Metropolitan of Lacedaemon, beheaded by the Turks in 1767.
4-15.name: Ananias of Lacedaemon

4-15.bio:
Theodore, a priest, and Pausolypios are commemorated together in the Greek synaxaria among the martyrs of the fifteenth of April. Little is preserved of their story beyond their confession of Christ and their death for the faith.

The Church keeps their names in her calendar.
4-15.desc: Holy Martyrs Theodore the Presbyter and Pausolypios.
4-15.name: Theodore the Presbyter and Pausolypios

4-15.bio:
Suchias and his companions were noblemen of Caucasian Albania who escorted a princess to Armenia and there came to faith in Christ. Leaving the court, they lived as ascetics in the mountains of Georgia.

When a new ruler demanded their return to paganism they refused, and tradition relates that they were burned alive in the second century.
4-15.desc: Holy Martyr Suchias and his companions, warriors who suffered for Christ in Georgia.
4-15.name: Suchias and the Martyrs of Georgia

4-16.bio:
The holy virgins Agape, Irene, and Chionia were sisters from the region of Thessaloniki who suffered in the year 304, during the persecution of Diocletian. Arrested for their faith and for keeping the holy Scriptures when the emperor had ordered them destroyed, they refused to eat food sacrificed to idols or deny Christ, standing firm through interrogation.

Agape and Chionia were burned, and Irene, after further trials, followed her sisters in martyrdom. Three sisters crowned as one, they are commemorated on April 16.
4-16.desc: Holy Martyrs Agape, Irene, and Chionia.
4-16.name: Irene, Agape & Chionia

4-16.bio:
These women of Corinth were brought to faith by the preaching of Leonides, Bishop of Athens, and were arrested with him in the persecution of Decius. They refused to deny Christ under torture.

Tradition relates that they were cast into the sea at Corinth in the third century, and that the Church of Corinth kept their memory with great honour, building a basilica over their tomb.
4-16.desc: Holy Women Martyrs Chariessa, Nike, Galene, Kalles, Nunechia, Basilissa, Theodora and Irene, drowned at Corinth with Bishop Leonides.
4-16.greek: Χάρισσα, Νίκη, Γαλήνη, Καλλίς, Νουνεχία, Βασίλισσα, Θεοδώρα και Ειρήνη
4-16.name: Chariessa, Nike, Galene and the Women Martyrs of Corinth

4-16.bio:
Michael was a youth from Vourla near Smyrna who, tradition relates, was tricked by Turks into uttering words of conversion while intoxicated. Coming to himself, he refused to accept Islam and boldly declared that he was a Christian.

He was beheaded at Smyrna in 1772, about eighteen years of age.
4-16.desc: Holy New Martyr Michael of Vourla, beheaded at Smyrna at the age of eighteen.
4-16.name: Michael of Vourla

4-16.bio:
Amphilochios was born on Patmos in 1889 and became a monk at the Monastery of Saint John the Theologian there, later serving as its abbot. He founded the Convent of the Annunciation on the island and laboured as a spiritual father throughout the Dodecanese, especially during the years of Italian occupation.

He was known for his gentleness, his love of trees and of all creation, and his gift of discernment. He reposed in 1970 and was numbered among the saints in 2018.
4-16.desc: Venerable Amphilochios Makris of Patmos, elder and founder of the Convent of the Annunciation.
4-16.name: Amphilochios of Patmos

4-16.bio:
Christopher was a monk of the Dionysiou Monastery on Mount Athos. Tradition relates that having in his youth outwardly accepted Islam under pressure, he repented, and after monastic preparation returned to confess Christ before the Ottoman judge.

He was beheaded at Adrianople in 1818 and is honoured among the Athonite new martyrs.
4-16.desc: Holy New Martyr Christopher, monk of the Dionysiou Monastery, martyred at Adrianople.
4-16.name: Christopher of Dionysiou

4-16.bio:
Michael was born in the Agrapha mountains and worked as a baker in Thessalonica. Tradition relates that a Turkish boy who was fond of him was heard praising Christ, and Michael was accused of leading him from Islam.

He confessed the faith before the judge and was burned alive in Thessalonica in 1544.
4-16.desc: Holy New Martyr Michael Mavroudis of Agrapha, burned at Thessalonica.
4-16.name: Michael Mavroudis

4-17.bio:
St. Ariadne was a Christian servant in Phrygia in the early centuries of the Church. When she refused to take part in the pagan festivities of her master's household, she was punished for her faith and pursued when she fled. Tradition relates that as her persecutors closed upon her she prayed, and a rock opened to receive her, taking her beyond their reach into the hands of God.

The Church honors her as a martyr in will and deed, a lowly servant whose faithfulness shamed the powerful. She is commemorated on April 17.
4-17.name: Ariadne

4-17.bio:
Simeon bar Sabbae was bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, the chief city of Persia, when King Shapur began his persecution of the Christians in the fourth century. Accused of loyalty to Rome and of refusing to worship the sun, he was arrested with many of his clergy.

Tradition relates that he was beheaded on Great Friday after watching a great multitude of his flock die before him, among them the priests Abdechalas and Ananias and the royal official Usthazanes.
4-17.desc: Hieromartyr Simeon, Bishop of Persia, and the many who suffered with him under Shapur.
4-17.name: Simeon of Persia and those with him

4-17.bio:
Adrian was a Christian of Corinth arrested during the persecution of Decius in the third century. Commanded to sacrifice to the idols, he refused and instead overturned the altar.

He was beaten and cast into a furnace, receiving the crown of martyrdom.
4-17.desc: Holy Martyr Adrian of Corinth, who was burned for Christ under Decius.
4-17.name: Adrian of Corinth

4-17.bio:
Makarios Notaras was born in Corinth in 1731 and was chosen Metropolitan of Corinth by his people. Removed from his see after the uprising of 1770, he devoted himself to the spiritual renewal of the Greek people, defending frequent Communion and the traditions of the Church.

With Saint Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain he gathered and published the Philokalia, and he prepared many new martyrs for their confession. He reposed on Chios in 1805.
4-17.desc: Saint Makarios Notaras, Metropolitan of Corinth, Kollyvades father and co-compiler of the Philokalia.
4-17.name: Makarios of Corinth

4-17.bio:
Agapetus was Bishop of Rome in the sixth century. Sent to Constantinople on an embassy by the Gothic king, he found the patriarchal throne occupied by Anthimus, a Monophysite, and refused communion with him until the emperor Justinian consented to his removal.

He consecrated Menas as Orthodox patriarch and died in Constantinople in 536, honoured by East and West alike.
4-17.desc: Saint Agapetus, Pope of Rome, who deposed the heretic Anthimus at Constantinople.
4-17.name: Agapetus of Rome

4-17.bio:
Azat was a favoured eunuch of the Persian court under King Shapur who confessed himself a Christian during the great persecution. Tradition relates that he was put to death together with a vast number of believers.

The king, grieved at the death of his servant, is said to have restrained the persecution thereafter.
4-17.desc: Holy Martyr Azat the Eunuch, official of the Persian court, with those who suffered with him.
4-17.name: Azat the Eunuch

4-17.bio:
Zosimas was a monk of the Russian north who, with Saint Herman, settled on the Solovki islands in the White Sea in the fifteenth century, on the site where Saint Sabbatius had lived before him. He built the first church there and became the first abbot of the community.

He guided the brotherhood through great hardship and reposed in 1478. Solovki became one of the great monasteries of Russia.
4-17.desc: Venerable Zosimas, abbot and co-founder of the Solovki Monastery in the White Sea.
4-17.name: Zosimas of Solovki

4-18.bio:
St. Cosmas the Confessor was Bishop of Chalcedon in the ninth century, during the second period of iconoclasm. Raised in the monastic life before his consecration, he refused to renounce the veneration of the holy icons when the emperor demanded it, and for this he was stripped of his see and endured persecution and exile.

He remained faithful to the end, and the Church numbers him among the confessor hierarchs through whom the Orthodox faith was preserved. He is commemorated on April 18.
4-18.desc: St. Cosmas the Confessor, Bishop of Chalcedon.
4-18.name: Cosmas, Bishop of Chalcedon

4-18.bio:
John was a disciple of Saint Gregory of Decapolis and shared his labours in defence of the holy icons during the ninth-century iconoclast persecution. He lived in stillness and prayer and was known for his humility.

After the death of his elder he continued the ascetic life in Constantinople and reposed in peace.
4-18.desc: Venerable John the Hesychast, disciple of Saint Gregory of Decapolis.
4-18.name: John the Hesychast

4-18.bio:
Athanasia was born on the island of Aegina in the ninth century and was twice married, the second time to a man who himself later became a monk. Freed to follow her heart's desire, she founded a convent on the island and was made its abbess.

She lived in great austerity and charity, was granted the gift of healing, and reposed in peace. Her relics were later found incorrupt.
4-18.desc: Venerable Athanasia of Aegina, abbess and wonderworker.
4-18.name: Athanasia of Aegina

4-18.bio:
John was born in Ioannina in Epirus and worked as a tailor in Constantinople among Christians who had accepted Islam. Pressed by them to do the same, he answered that he had been born a Christian and would die one.

After imprisonment and torture he was burned at Constantinople in 1526, and is honoured as the first of the new martyrs of Epirus.
4-18.desc: Holy New Martyr John of Ioannina, a tailor burned for Christ in Constantinople.
4-18.name: John the Tailor of Ioannina

4-18.bio:
Akakios was Bishop of Melitene in Armenia in the fifth century and took part in the Third Ecumenical Council at Ephesus, where he opposed the teaching of Nestorius. He was known for his gift of working wonders and his care for his flock.

He reposed in peace and was buried at Melitene.
4-18.desc: Saint Akakios, Bishop of Melitene, wonderworker and father of the Third Ecumenical Council.
4-18.name: Akakios of Melitene

4-18.bio:
Cyril was born in Adrianople in the eighteenth century and served as Ecumenical Patriarch from 1810 to 1812, caring especially for the education of the clergy. After his resignation he lived quietly in his native city.

When the Greek revolution broke out in 1821 he was seized by the Ottomans and hanged at the gate of the cathedral of Adrianople. He is honoured as a hieromartyr of the Great Church.
4-18.desc: Hieromartyr Cyril VI, Patriarch of Constantinople, hanged at Adrianople in 1821.
4-18.name: Cyril VI of Constantinople

4-18.bio:
The Kollyvades were a movement of Athonite fathers of the eighteenth century, among them Makarios of Corinth, Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain and Athanasios of Paros, who called the faithful back to the Church's tradition of frequent Communion, watchfulness and the prayer of the heart.

Mocked at first for their strictness about memorial services on Sundays, they became through the Philokalia and their other writings the spiritual renewers of Orthodoxy under Ottoman rule.
4-18.desc: Synaxis of the holy Kollyvades Fathers of Mount Athos, renewers of the spiritual life of the Greek people.
4-18.name: Synaxis of the Kollyvades Fathers

4-19.bio:
St. John of the Ladder gave his whole life to Mount Sinai, entering the monastery there in his youth, living long years as a hermit in the desert nearby, and at last serving as abbot of the holy mountain of Moses. From the depths of his experience he wrote The Ladder of Divine Ascent, a guide of thirty steps by which the soul climbs from renunciation of the world to the summit of faith, hope, and love.

His book remains a cornerstone of Orthodox spiritual life, read aloud in monasteries each Great Lent. He is commemorated on April 19.
4-19.desc: Abbot of Sinai and author of The Ladder of Divine Ascent.
4-19.name: John of the Ladder

4-19.bio:
Paphnutius is commemorated in the synaxaria as a hieromartyr of Jerusalem who suffered many torments and was put to death for Christ. The details of his life have not been preserved.

He is distinct from the several other saints named Paphnutius, including the confessor of Egypt honoured in September.
4-19.name: Paphnutius of Jerusalem

4-19.bio:
Theodore was a young soldier of Perge in Pamphylia who refused to sacrifice to the idols and was cruelly tortured in the second century. The pagan priest Dioscorus, seeing his endurance, believed in Christ and was burned; the soldiers Socrates and Dionysius who guarded him likewise confessed and were speared.

Theodore was crucified, and his mother Philippa, who stood by him, was beheaded. They are honoured together.
4-19.desc: Holy Martyrs Theodore of Perge, his mother Philippa, and Dioscorus, Socrates and Dionysius.
4-19.name: Theodore of Perge and those with him

4-19.bio:
Agathangelos was born Athanasios in Thrace and, working as a sailor, was pressed into accepting Islam by the Turks. Repenting, he fled to Mount Athos and became a monk at Esphigmenou, where he prepared himself to confess the faith he had denied.

He returned to Smyrna, publicly declared himself a Christian, and was beheaded there in 1819.
4-19.desc: Holy New Martyr Agathangelos of the Esphigmenou Monastery, beheaded at Smyrna.
4-19.name: Agathangelos of Esphigmenou

4-19.bio:
George was a monk who became Bishop of Antioch in Pisidia in the ninth century. When the emperor Leo the Armenian renewed the iconoclast persecution, George refused to reject the holy icons.

He was driven from his see and died in exile, honoured as a confessor.
4-19.desc: Saint George the Confessor, Bishop of Antioch in Pisidia, who suffered exile for the icons.
4-19.name: George of Pisidia

4-19.bio:
Tryphon was a monk chosen Patriarch of Constantinople in the tenth century, to hold the throne until the emperor's young son Theophylact came of age. He governed the Church with piety and simplicity.

Tradition relates that he was removed from the throne through a stratagem of the emperor's officials; he returned to his monastery without complaint and reposed in peace.
4-19.desc: Saint Tryphon, Patriarch of Constantinople, who yielded his throne in humility.
4-19.name: Tryphon of Constantinople

4-19.bio:
Symeon was abbot of the Philotheou Monastery on Mount Athos in the sixteenth century. Leaving the Holy Mountain, he travelled barefoot and in a single tunic through Thessaly, Euboea and the mainland preaching repentance, and founded the Monastery of Flamouri on Mount Pelion.

He reposed in peace and is honoured among the Athonite saints.
4-19.desc: Venerable Symeon the Barefoot of Philotheou, abbot and preacher of repentance in Greece.
4-19.name: Symeon of Philotheou

4-2.bio:
St. Titus the Wonderworker was a monk who from his youth gave himself to the ascetic life, excelling in obedience, humility, and love for the brethren. He served Christ in a monastic brotherhood, and for the purity of his life he received from God the grace of working wonders, from which he takes his title.

The synaxaria preserve few details of his story, but the Church keeps his memory as one of the quiet venerable fathers whose hidden labors adorned the monastic life. He is commemorated on April 2.
4-2.name: Titus the Wonderworker

4-2.bio:
Amphianus and Edesius were brothers from Patara in Lycia, sent to Beirut to study, who there came to the Christian faith. Amphianus went to Caesarea in Palestine, where he publicly rebuked the governor for sacrificing to idols and, after torture, was drowned in the sea.

Edesius was sent to labour in the mines and was later martyred at Alexandria, tradition relates, for rebuking a judge who was abusing Christian women. Both suffered in the early fourth century.
4-2.desc: Holy Martyrs Amphianus and Edesius, brothers from Patara in Lycia who suffered under Maximinus.
4-2.name: Amphianus and Edesius of Lycia

4-2.bio:
Polycarp was a Christian of Alexandria who, seeing the blood of the martyrs shed in his city under the emperor Maximian, openly denounced the persecution. He was seized, tortured, and executed for his boldness.

He is not to be confused with the great hieromartyr Polycarp of Smyrna, commemorated in February.
4-2.desc: Holy Martyr Polycarp of Alexandria, who rebuked the persecutor and was put to death.
4-2.name: Polycarp of Alexandria

4-2.bio:
Theodora was a young Christian woman of Tyre in Phoenicia who, at about seventeen years of age, boldly confessed her faith before Urban, the governor of Palestine, during the persecution of the early fourth century.

After cruel torture she was cast into the sea. The synaxaria honour her among the virgin martyrs of the age of Diocletian.
4-2.desc: Holy Virgin Martyr Theodora of Tyre, a maiden of seventeen who confessed Christ before the governor of Palestine.
4-2.name: Theodora of Tyre

4-2.bio:
Gregory is remembered in the Greek synaxaria as an ascetic who practised the monastic life in the region of Nicomedia in Bithynia. Tradition relates that he lived in quiet stillness and prayer and reposed in peace.

Few details of his life have been preserved beyond his name and the place of his struggles.
4-2.desc: Venerable Gregory, who lived the ascetic life near Nicomedia.
4-2.name: Gregory of Nicomedia

4-2.bio:
George was a Georgian hierarch who served as Bishop of Atsquri in the south-west of Georgia around the end of the ninth and beginning of the tenth centuries. He is remembered in the writings of the Georgian hagiographers of that period as a holy and learned pastor.

He is venerated by the Georgian Church and appears in the Greek synaxaria on this day.
4-2.desc: Saint George Matskvereli, Bishop of Atsquri in Georgia.
4-2.name: George of Atsquri

4-20.bio:
St. Theodore Trichinas was born in Constantinople and embraced the monastic life in a monastery of the countryside. He is called Trichinas, the hair-shirt wearer, because his only garment throughout his long ascetic struggle was a rough covering of hair, worn in every season as he mortified the flesh through fasting, vigil, and cold.

God glorified his hidden labors with the grace of wonders, and after his repose the faithful continued to receive healing at his relics. He is commemorated on April 20.
4-20.desc: Venerable Theodore Trichinas, the Hair-shirt Wearer.
4-20.name: Theodore Trichinas

4-20.bio:
Zacchaeus was the chief tax collector of Jericho who, being short of stature, climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus and was called down to receive Him in his house, where he promised to restore fourfold all he had taken unjustly.

Tradition relates that he later followed the Apostle Peter and became bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, where he reposed in peace.
4-20.desc: Holy Apostle Zacchaeus, the tax collector of Jericho who received the Lord in his house.
4-20.name: Zacchaeus the Apostle

4-20.bio:
Athanasios was born in Hypate in the fourteenth century and became a monk on Mount Athos. Fleeing pirate raids, he came to the rocks of Meteora in Thessaly, where he climbed the great pillar of stone and founded the Monastery of the Transfiguration, the Great Meteoron.

He gave his community its rule and reposed in peace, having established one of the great monastic centres of Greece.
4-20.desc: Venerable Athanasios, founder of the Great Meteoron monastery on the rocks of Thessaly.
4-20.name: Athanasios of Meteora

4-20.bio:
These men were witnesses of the sufferings of the Great Martyr George at Nicomedia and, seeing his endurance and the wonders worked through him, believed in Christ and confessed openly before the emperor.

They were put to death at the beginning of the fourth century and are honoured together with the other converts of Saint George's martyrdom.
4-20.desc: Holy Martyrs Victor, Zoticus, Acindynus, Caesarius, Severian, Christopher, Theonas and Antoninus of Nicomedia.
4-20.greek: Βίκτωρ, Ζωτικός, Ακίνδυνος, Καισάριος, Σεβηριανός, Χριστόφορος, Θεωνάς και Αντωνίνος
4-20.name: Martyrs of Nicomedia converted by Saint George

4-20.bio:
John was a monk of the Old Lavra founded by Saint Chariton in the Judaean desert. He lived in asceticism and prayer, tradition relates, in the eighth century, and was known for his humility.

He reposed in peace in the desert of Palestine.
4-20.desc: Venerable John of the Old Lavra of Saint Chariton in Palestine.
4-20.name: John of the Old Lavra

4-20.bio:
Joasaph was born John Uros, son of the Serbian ruler of Thessaly, and inherited his father's throne while young. Renouncing worldly power, he went up to Meteora and became a disciple of Saint Athanasios, who named him his successor.

He enlarged the Great Meteoron and guided its brotherhood, reposing in peace in the early fifteenth century.
4-20.desc: Venerable Joasaph of Meteora, a prince who left his throne for the monastic life.
4-20.name: Joasaph of Meteora

4-20.bio:
Gabriel was a child of a peasant family near Bialystok who, tradition relates, was abducted and killed at the age of six in 1690. His body was found some time later and his relics remained incorrupt.

He is venerated in Poland and Belarus as a protector of children.
4-20.name: Gabriel of Bialystok

4-21.bio:
St. Anastasios was Patriarch of Antioch in the sixth century, a theologian and ascetic who shepherded one of the great sees of the East in a turbulent age. Standing firm for the Orthodox teaching on the Incarnation against imperial pressure, he was driven from his throne and endured long years of exile before being restored to his flock.

The Church honors him among the confessor hierarchs who preferred banishment to the least compromise of the faith. He is commemorated on April 21.
4-21.name: Anastasios of Antioch

4-21.bio:
Januarius was Bishop of Benevento in Italy at the time of the persecution of Diocletian. Visiting his deacon Sosius in prison, he was himself arrested with the deacons Proculus and Faustus and others.

Tradition relates that they were thrown to the beasts unharmed and were finally beheaded at Pozzuoli in the early fourth century. His relics are venerated at Naples.
4-21.desc: Hieromartyr Januarius, Bishop of Benevento, with the deacons Proculus, Sosius and Faustus and their companions.
4-21.name: Januarius of Benevento and his companions

4-21.bio:
Alexandra was, according to tradition, the wife of the emperor Diocletian. Witnessing the tortures of the Great Martyr George and the wonders wrought through him, she openly declared herself a Christian before her husband.

Condemned to death with George, she died on the way to execution, and her servants Apollo, Isaacius and Codratus were martyred for their faith soon after.
4-21.desc: Holy Martyr Alexandra the Empress, who confessed Christ at the martyrdom of Saint George, with her servants Apollo, Isaacius and Codratus.
4-21.name: Alexandra the Empress

4-21.bio:
Maximian was a priest of Constantinople known for his charity, who had used his wealth to build tombs for the poor. After Nestorius was condemned at the Third Ecumenical Council he was chosen patriarch in his place.

He governed the Church in peace for a few years and reposed in the fifth century.
4-21.desc: Saint Maximian, Patriarch of Constantinople, successor of the deposed Nestorius.
4-21.name: Maximian of Constantinople

4-21.bio:
Anastasios was a monk and later abbot of the Monastery of Saint Catherine on Mount Sinai in the seventh century. He travelled widely in Egypt and Syria disputing with heretics and wrote works of theology and spiritual guidance.

He reposed in peace at an advanced age.
4-21.desc: Venerable Anastasios the Sinaite, abbot of Mount Sinai and defender of the faith.
4-21.name: Anastasios the Sinaite

4-22.bio:
St. Theodore of Sykeon was born in a village of Galatia in Asia Minor in the sixth century. Given to prayer and fasting from childhood, he became a monk of extraordinary asceticism, and his holiness drew crowds seeking healing and counsel; against his will he was made a bishop, though he later returned to his beloved monastic quiet.

Famed as a wonderworker in his own lifetime, he was sought out by emperors and peasants alike, and reposed early in the seventh century. He is commemorated on April 22.
4-22.name: Theodore Sykeon

4-22.bio:
Nathanael of Cana in Galilee was brought to Jesus by Philip and, hearing that the Lord had seen him under the fig tree, confessed Him as the Son of God. He was among the disciples to whom the risen Christ appeared at the Sea of Tiberias.

The Church has generally identified him with the Apostle Bartholomew, one of the Twelve.
4-22.desc: Holy Apostle Nathanael, the Israelite in whom there was no guile.
4-22.name: Nathanael the Apostle

4-22.bio:
Nearchos was a soldier at Melitene in Armenia and the close friend of Polyeuctus, whom he brought to faith in Christ before Polyeuctus's own martyrdom. He later confessed the faith himself.

Tradition relates that he was burned alive in the third century.
4-22.desc: Holy Martyr Nearchos, the friend of Saint Polyeuctus, burned for Christ.
4-22.name: Nearchos the Martyr

4-22.bio:
Gaius was Bishop of Rome at the end of the third century, a Dalmatian by birth and, tradition relates, a kinsman of the emperor Diocletian. He guided the Church through the years before the great persecution.

He reposed in 296 and is honoured among the holy popes of old Rome.
4-22.desc: Saint Gaius, Pope of Rome, who suffered under Diocletian.
4-22.name: Gaius of Rome

4-22.bio:
Gregory Gravanos was a Christian of the island of Nisyros in the Dodecanese who, in the years of Ottoman rule, confessed Christ before the authorities and was put to death.

He is honoured by the faithful of his island among the new martyrs.
4-22.desc: Holy New Martyr Gregory Gravanos of the island of Nisyros.
4-22.name: Gregory Gravanos of Nisyros

4-22.bio:
Platon Jovanovic was a Serbian hierarch who became Bishop of Banja Luka in Bosnia. When the Ustasha regime came to power in 1941 he refused to abandon his flock.

He was arrested, tortured and killed, his body thrown into the river Vrbas. He is honoured as a hieromartyr of the Serbian Church.
4-22.desc: Hieromartyr Platon, Bishop of Banja Luka, murdered in 1941.
4-22.name: Platon of Banja Luka

4-23.bio:
St. George the Great Martyr and Trophy-Bearer was a Roman officer from Cappadocia who suffered for Christ under the Emperor Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century. Confessing his faith openly before the emperor, he endured many tortures and was beheaded, and his courage brought many to belief.

One of the most venerated saints in both East and West, he is honored as patron of soldiers and invoked as a swift helper in danger. Tradition depicts him as the dragon-slayer, an image of faith triumphing over evil. His feast on April 23 is one of the great name days of the Greek world; when it falls before Pascha it is transferred to Bright Monday.
4-23.desc: Great Martyr George the Trophy-Bearer, patron of soldiers.
4-23.name: George the Great Martyr

4-23.bio:
Glykerios was a poor farmer whose ox had died and who, tradition relates, was restored to prosperity through the prayer of the Great Martyr George in prison. He confessed Christ openly.

He was beheaded at Nicomedia at the beginning of the fourth century.
4-23.desc: Holy Martyr Glykerios the Farmer, who believed at the martyrdom of Saint George.
4-23.name: Glykerios the Farmer

4-23.bio:
Anatolios and Protoleon were officers of the imperial army who witnessed the endurance of the Great Martyr George under torture and the wonders worked through him. They declared themselves Christians before the emperor.

They were beheaded at Nicomedia in the early fourth century.
4-23.desc: Holy Martyrs Anatolios and Protoleon, soldiers who confessed Christ at the martyrdom of Saint George.
4-23.name: Anatolios and Protoleon

4-23.bio:
Athanasios was a sorcerer summoned by the emperor to overcome the Great Martyr George by poison. When the poison did George no harm, Athanasios fell at his feet and confessed Christ.

He was beheaded at once and received the crown of martyrdom.
4-23.desc: Holy Martyr Athanasios, the sorcerer who was converted at the martyrdom of Saint George.
4-23.name: Athanasios the Magician

4-23.bio:
George was a Cypriot who worked in Ptolemais in Palestine, where a false accusation was brought against him by the Turks. Urged to save himself by embracing Islam, he refused.

He was beheaded at Ptolemais in 1752 and is honoured among the new martyrs of Cyprus.
4-23.desc: Holy New Martyr George the Cypriot, martyred at Ptolemais.
4-23.name: George the Cypriot

4-23.bio:
Lazarus was a Bulgarian shepherd who came to work in Asia Minor near Pergamon. Falsely accused by a Turkish woman, he was pressed to accept Islam and refused, confessing Christ under torture.

He was put to death in 1802 and is honoured by the Bulgarian and Greek Churches alike.
4-23.desc: Holy New Martyr Lazarus the Shepherd of Bulgaria, martyred near Pergamon.
4-23.name: Lazarus of Bulgaria

4-23.bio:
Polychronia, according to tradition, was the mother of the Great Martyr George, a Christian of Palestine who raised her son in the faith after his father's death.

The Greek synaxaria commemorate her with her son, relating that she too suffered for Christ in the persecution of Diocletian.
4-23.desc: Holy Martyr Polychronia, mother of the Great Martyr George.
4-23.name: Polychronia the Martyr

4-24.bio:
St. Elizabeth was a holy woman of Constantinople who from her youth gave herself wholly to God in the monastic life. Excelling in fasting, vigil, and compassion for the poor, she became the spiritual mother of a community of nuns, and the faithful sought her prayers, through which many received healing.

Her memory has been kept in the Church from ancient times as an image of quiet, hidden sanctity bearing abundant fruit. She is commemorated on April 24.
4-24.name: Elizabeth

4-24.bio:
St. Simeon Stylites the Younger was born in Antioch in the sixth century. Drawn to asceticism from early childhood, he took up the extraordinary struggle of the pillar-dwellers, living for the greater part of his long life atop a column on the mountain near Antioch called the Wonderful Mountain, in unceasing prayer and fasting.

A priest and wonderworker, he counseled and healed the multitudes who climbed to him, and a monastery grew up around his pillar. He reposed in old age near the end of the sixth century, and is commemorated on April 24.
4-24.name: Simeon Stylites the Younger

4-24.bio:
Sabbas was a Goth who rose to the rank of military commander at Rome under the emperor Aurelian. A Christian, he visited and cared for the imprisoned confessors, and when denounced he laid aside his belt of office and declared his faith.

Seventy soldiers, seeing the wonders wrought during his tortures, believed and were beheaded; Sabbas himself was drowned in the Tiber in 272.
4-24.desc: Holy Martyr Sabbas the General, a Goth by birth, drowned in the Tiber with seventy soldiers.
4-24.name: Sabbas Stratelates

4-24.bio:
Xenophon was an Athonite ascetic who, tradition relates, founded the monastery that bears his name on the western shore of the Holy Mountain, dedicated to the Great Martyr George, in the tenth century.

He reposed in peace and is honoured among the founders of Athos.
4-24.desc: Venerable Xenophon, founder of the Monastery of Xenophontos on Mount Athos.
4-24.name: Xenophon of Athos

4-24.bio:
Doukas was a tailor from Mytilene working in Constantinople. Tradition relates that a Turkish woman who desired him accused him falsely when he refused her, and he was ordered to embrace Islam.

He firmly confessed Christ and was flayed alive in 1564.
4-24.desc: Holy New Martyr Doukas the Tailor of Mytilene, flayed for Christ in Constantinople.
4-24.name: Doukas of Mytilene

4-24.bio:
Nicholas was a young Christian of Magnesia near Smyrna in the service of a Turkish landowner, who pressed him to accept Islam. He refused and confessed Christ.

He was beaten to death in 1796 and is honoured among the new martyrs of Asia Minor.
4-24.desc: Holy New Martyr Nicholas of Magnesia in Asia Minor.
4-24.name: Nicholas of Magnesia

4-24.bio:
Pasicrates and Valentio were soldiers of the garrison at Dorostolum on the Danube who refused to offer incense to the idols. Tradition relates that Pasicrates, ordered to sacrifice, cast the incense away and declared his faith.

They were beheaded at the end of the third century.
4-24.desc: Holy Martyrs Pasicrates and Valentio, soldiers beheaded at Dorostolum in Moesia.
4-24.name: Pasicrates and Valentio

4-24.bio:
Thomas was a monk of a Syrian monastery who was sent to Antioch on the affairs of his community and there took up the life of a fool for Christ, enduring mockery for the love of God. Tradition relates that wonders followed his death in the sixth century.

He is one of the early holy fools honoured by the Church.
4-24.desc: Venerable Thomas the Fool for Christ of Syria.
4-24.name: Thomas the Fool for Christ

4-25.bio:
St. Mark the Evangelist, one of the Seventy, was a companion of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and wrote the second Gospel, which ancient tradition holds preserves the preaching of Peter. He labored in the spread of the Gospel from Jerusalem to Rome, and is honored as the founder of the Church of Alexandria in Egypt.

There, according to tradition, he was seized by the pagans and dragged through the streets, completing his apostolic course as a martyr. The father of one of the great ancient Churches, he is commemorated on April 25.
4-25.name: Mark the Evangelist

4-25.bio:
Nike is listed in the Greek synaxaria as a martyr who gave her life for Christ. Little of her story has been preserved beyond her name and her witness.

Her memory on this day is kept by the many Greek women who bear her name.
4-25.desc: Holy Martyr Nike, commemorated on this day in the Greek synaxaria.
4-25.name: Nike the Martyr

4-25.bio:
Macedonius was Patriarch of Constantinople at the end of the fifth century, a man of ascetic life and firm Orthodoxy. When the emperor Anastasius pressed him to reject the Council of Chalcedon he refused.

He was deposed and exiled to Euchaita, where he reposed in the sixth century, honoured as a confessor.
4-25.desc: Saint Macedonius II, Patriarch of Constantinople, exiled for defending the Council of Chalcedon.
4-25.name: Macedonius II of Constantinople

4-25.bio:
Anianus was a cobbler of Alexandria who, tradition relates, wounded his hand while mending the sandal of the Apostle Mark and was healed by him, whereupon he and his household believed in Christ.

Mark ordained him bishop, and after the apostle's martyrdom he governed the Church of Alexandria until his own repose in the first century.
4-25.desc: Saint Anianus, second Bishop of Alexandria, converted by the Apostle Mark.
4-25.name: Anianus of Alexandria

4-25.bio:
Sylvester was a disciple of Saint Sergius of Radonezh who withdrew to the forests by the river Obnora in northern Russia in the fourteenth century. Disciples gathered around him and a monastery of the Resurrection was founded there.

He reposed in 1379 and his relics are venerated at his monastery.
4-25.desc: Venerable Sylvester of Obnora, disciple of Saint Sergius of Radonezh.
4-25.name: Sylvester of Obnora

4-25.bio:
Basil was a monk who settled in the mountains of Wallachia in the eighteenth century and founded the hermitage of Poiana Marului, gathering a community devoted to inner prayer and the study of the fathers.

He was the spiritual father of Saint Paisius Velichkovsky and wrote introductions to the works of the hesychast fathers. He reposed in 1767.
4-25.desc: Venerable Basil of Poiana Marului, Romanian elder and teacher of the prayer of the heart.
4-25.name: Basil of Poiana Marului

4-26.bio:
St. Basil was Bishop of Amaseia in Pontus in the early fourth century, in the last days of the persecutions. A fearless shepherd who protected those who fled to the Church for refuge, he drew upon himself the anger of the emperor Licinius, and was put to death for his faithfulness, his body cast into the sea.

Tradition relates that his relics were recovered by the faithful and buried with honor in his own city. The Church commemorates him on April 26.
4-26.name: Basil of Amaseia

4-26.bio:
Glaphyra was a maidservant of the empress Constantia, wife of Licinius. When the emperor sought to seduce her, the empress helped her flee in disguise to Amaseia, where Bishop Basil received her and she gave money to build a church.

When her whereabouts were discovered she was condemned with Basil, but reposed before the sentence could be carried out, in the early fourth century.
4-26.desc: Holy Virgin Glaphyra, servant of the empress, who fled to Amaseia and was sheltered by Saint Basil.
4-26.name: Glaphyra the Virgin

4-26.bio:
Stephen was born in Ustyug in the fourteenth century and became a monk in Rostov, where he learned Greek and the language of the pagan Zyrians of the north. Going among them as a missionary, he created an alphabet for their tongue and translated the services.

He was made first Bishop of Perm, built churches and schools, and reposed in Moscow in 1396.
4-26.desc: Saint Stephen, Bishop of Perm, enlightener of the Zyrian people.
4-26.name: Stephen of Perm

4-26.bio:
Leo is commemorated in the Greek synaxaria as a holy bishop of the island of Samos who shepherded his flock in piety and reposed in peace. The details of his life have not been preserved.

He is venerated among the local saints of the eastern Aegean.
4-26.name: Leo of Samos

4-26.bio:
Tamara reigned over Georgia from 1184 to 1213, a time of peace, learning and church-building remembered as the golden age of the kingdom. She was renowned for her piety, her justice and her generosity to monasteries and the poor.

She reposed in 1213 and is honoured by the Georgian Church, which keeps her memory also on the first of May.
4-26.desc: Holy Queen Tamara of Georgia, under whom the Georgian kingdom reached its golden age.
4-26.name: Tamara the Queen

4-26.bio:
George, a priest of the village of Gergeri in Crete, and twelve of his fellow villagers were put to death by the Turks for their faith during the years of Ottoman rule.

They are honoured together by the Church of Crete.
4-26.desc: Holy New Martyrs George the Presbyter and the twelve with him at Gergeri in Crete.
4-26.greek: Γεώργιος ο Πρεσβύτερος και οι Δώδεκα Νεομάρτυρες Γέργερης
4-26.name: George of Gergeri and the Twelve New Martyrs

4-27.bio:
St. Simeon was a kinsman of the Lord according to the flesh, the son of Clopas, and became the second Bishop of Jerusalem after the death of James the Brother of God. He shepherded the mother Church of Jerusalem through decades of trial, including the destruction of the city, guarding the flock of Christ in the very places of His Passion and Resurrection.

In extreme old age he was denounced to the Romans, and after enduring tortures was crucified in the days of the emperor Trajan, following his Lord in the manner of his death. He is commemorated on April 27.
4-27.desc: Hieromartyr Simeon, Kinsman of the Lord, Bishop of Jerusalem.
4-27.name: Simeon, Bishop of Jerusalem

4-27.bio:
John was abbot of the Monastery of Kathares in Bithynia in the ninth century. When the iconoclast emperors renewed their persecution he refused to renounce the holy icons and was imprisoned, scourged and exiled.

He endured many years of hardship and reposed in peace, honoured as a confessor.
4-27.desc: Venerable John the Confessor, abbot of the Monastery of Kathares, who suffered for the icons.
4-27.name: John of Kathares

4-27.bio:
Poplion is commemorated in the Greek synaxaria as a martyr who gave his life for Christ. Nothing further of his life has been preserved.

The Church keeps his name in her calendar on this day.
4-27.name: Poplion the Martyr

4-27.bio:
Eulogius was a stonecutter of Egypt who spent each day's wages in feeding and lodging the poor and travellers. Tradition relates that a holy elder prayed for him to receive wealth so that he might do more good, but riches led him astray until, at the elder's further prayer, he lost them and returned to his former humble life.

He reposed in peace and is honoured as a model of hospitality.
4-27.desc: Righteous Eulogius the Hospitable, a stonecutter who shared all he earned with strangers.
4-27.name: Eulogius the Hospitable

4-27.bio:
Lollion is commemorated in the Greek synaxaria as a martyr who was put to death for Christ. The details of his life have not been preserved.

He is one of the many martyrs whose memory the Church keeps by name alone.
4-27.name: Lollion the New

4-27.bio:
Stephen was a disciple of Saint Theodosius of the Kiev Caves and succeeded him as abbot of the monastery in the eleventh century, completing the great church he had begun. Later he founded a monastery of his own near Kiev.

He was made Bishop of Vladimir in Volhynia and reposed in 1094.
4-27.desc: Saint Stephen, abbot of the Kiev Caves and Bishop of Vladimir in Volhynia.
4-27.name: Stephen of Vladimir

4-28.bio:
The holy Apostles Jason and Sosipater were of the Seventy, kinsmen and fellow laborers of the Apostle Paul, who greets them in his Epistle to the Romans. According to tradition they carried the Gospel to the island of Kerkyra, where they preached, endured imprisonment, and converted many to Christ, including members of the ruling house.

They are honored as the founders and enlighteners of the Church of Corfu, where their veneration has continued unbroken since ancient times. They are commemorated together on April 28.
4-28.desc: Holy Apostles of the Seventy Jason and Sosipater.
4-28.name: Apostles Jason & Sosipater

4-28.bio:
Memnon was a monk and abbot in Egypt who was granted the gift of working wonders. Tradition relates that by his prayer a spring of water appeared in a dry place and locusts were driven from the fields.

He reposed in peace and was honoured by the faithful of his region.
4-28.desc: Venerable Memnon the Wonderworker, abbot in Egypt.
4-28.name: Memnon the Wonderworker

4-28.bio:
Cyril was born in Turov in the twelfth century and became a monk, living for a time as a stylite. Chosen bishop of his native city, he became famous for his sermons and prayers, which earned him the name of the Russian Chrysostom.

He reposed in peace toward the end of the twelfth century.
4-28.desc: Saint Cyril, Bishop of Turov, preacher and hymnographer of the Russian land.
4-28.name: Cyril of Turov

4-28.bio:
Auxibius is remembered in the Greek synaxaria as a venerable ascetic who lived in prayer and reposed in peace. The details of his life have not been preserved.

He is distinct from the hierarch Auxibius of Soloi in Cyprus, commemorated in February.
4-28.desc: Venerable Auxibius, ascetic commemorated in the Greek synaxaria.
4-28.name: Auxibius the Venerable

4-28.bio:
Agathon is listed in the Greek synaxaria as a venerable father who lived the monastic life and reposed in peace. His story has not been preserved beyond his name.

He is one of several ascetics of this name honoured by the Church.
4-28.desc: Venerable Agathon, ascetic commemorated on this day.
4-28.name: Agathon the Venerable

4-29.bio:
The holy Nine Martyrs suffered at Cyzicus, a city on the southern shore of the Sea of Marmara, during the persecutions of the third century. Christians of different ages and walks of life, they confessed Christ openly before the authorities, and when neither threats nor torments could move them, all nine were beheaded together.

When peace came to the Church their relics were found incorrupt, and a church was raised over them; many healings were received there by the faithful. They are commemorated on April 29.
4-29.desc: The Holy Nine Martyrs of Cyzicus.
4-29.name: Nine Martyrs of Cyzicus

4-29.bio:
Kerkyra was the daughter of the ruler of the island of Corfu at the time the Apostles Jason and Sosipater preached there. Seeing the endurance of the martyrs, she believed in Christ and gave her jewels to the poor.

Her father had her shut up and finally put to death, tradition relating that she was shot with arrows, in the first century. The island's cathedral keeps her memory.
4-29.desc: Holy Virgin Martyr Kerkyra, daughter of the king of Corfu, converted by the Apostles Jason and Sosipater.
4-29.name: Kerkyra the Martyr

4-29.bio:
John Kaloktenis was Metropolitan of Thebes in Boeotia in the twelfth century, remembered for his charity to the poor and for public works in his city, including water channels and hospitals.

He reposed in peace and is honoured by the Church of Thebes as its patron.
4-29.desc: Saint John Kaloktenis, Metropolitan of Thebes, the New Merciful One.
4-29.name: John Kaloktenis of Thebes

4-29.bio:
Eusebius, Zeno, Vitalius and Neon were among those converted on the island of Corfu by the preaching of the Apostles Jason and Sosipater. When they confessed Christ before the ruler they were condemned.

Tradition relates that they were burned alive in the first century.
4-29.desc: Holy Martyrs Eusebius, Zeno, Vitalius and Neon, who suffered at Corfu with the Apostles Jason and Sosipater.
4-29.name: Eusebius, Zeno, Vitalius and Neon

4-29.bio:
Saturninus, Iakischolus, Faustianus, Januarius, Marsalius, Euphrasius and Mammius were seven robbers imprisoned on Corfu together with the Apostles Jason and Sosipater. Through the apostles' teaching they came to faith in Christ.

They were put to death in a cauldron of boiling pitch in the first century and are honoured as the first martyrs of the island.
4-29.desc: The Holy Seven Martyrs of Corfu, robbers who believed in prison and were martyred in boiling pitch.
4-29.name: Seven Martyrs of Corfu

4-29.bio:
Christodoulos was an Ethiopian in the service of the ruler of Corfu who, seeing the wonders that accompanied the preaching of the Apostles Jason and Sosipater, believed in Christ and confessed openly.

He was put to death for his faith in the first century and is honoured with the other martyrs of Corfu.
4-29.desc: Holy Martyr Christodoulos the Ethiopian, who believed at Corfu and was martyred.
4-29.name: Christodoulos the Ethiopian

4-29.bio:
Basil was born in Herzegovina in the seventeenth century and became a monk and later Bishop of Zahumlje. Persecuted by the Turks and by Latin missionaries, he withdrew to the rock monastery of Ostrog in Montenegro, where he lived in great asceticism.

He reposed in 1671 and his relics remain incorrupt at Ostrog, where countless healings are attributed to his prayers.
4-29.desc: Saint Basil of Ostrog, Bishop of Zahumlje, wonderworker of Montenegro.
4-29.name: Basil of Ostrog

4-3.bio:
St. Nicetas the Confessor was abbot of the monastery of Medikion in Bithynia in the late eighth and early ninth centuries. A gentle father to his monks, he guided his community in prayer and asceticism until the renewal of iconoclasm, when he refused to reject the holy icons and was imprisoned and exiled by the emperor.

He endured his sufferings with patience and reposed a confessor, honored throughout the Church for his steadfastness in the Orthodox faith. He is commemorated on April 3.
4-3.desc: Venerable Nicetas the Confessor, Abbot of Medikion.
4-3.name: Nicetas the Confessor

4-3.bio:
Joseph was born in Sicily in the ninth century and, fleeing the Arab invasions, became a monk in Thessalonica and later in Constantinople. Sent on a mission to Rome, he was captured by pirates and held on Crete, where tradition relates he strengthened the faith of his fellow captives.

Returning to Constantinople he founded a monastery and composed a vast number of canons and hymns still sung in the Church. He suffered exile for the holy icons and reposed in peace, remembered as the sweet-voiced nightingale of the Church.
4-3.desc: Venerable Joseph the Hymnographer, composer of many canons of the Church and confessor for the holy icons.
4-3.name: Joseph the Hymnographer

4-3.bio:
These four martyrs are commemorated together in the synaxaria. Tradition relates that each met a different death for the faith: Elpidephoros was beheaded, Dius was stoned, Bithonius was drowned in the sea, and Galycus was given to wild beasts.

No further details of their lives have been preserved, but their names remain in the calendar of the Church.
4-3.desc: Holy Martyrs Elpidephoros, Dius, Bithonius and Galycus, who suffered different deaths for Christ.
4-3.name: Elpidephoros, Dius, Bithonius and Galycus

4-3.bio:
Illyrios devoted himself to ascetic struggle on Mount Myrsinon in the Peloponnese, where he is remembered as a wonderworker. The dates of his life are not known.

He is one of the many hermits of Greece whose memory survives chiefly through the veneration of the local faithful.
4-3.desc: Venerable Illyrios the Wonderworker, ascetic of Mount Myrsinon in the Peloponnese.
4-3.name: Illyrios of Mount Myrsinon

4-3.bio:
Paul was a Russian who had been taken captive by the Tatars and sold into slavery in Constantinople, where he was later ransomed and set free. Tradition relates that he was subject to fits, and during one of them Turks claimed he had professed Islam.

When he recovered he firmly refused to deny Christ, and was beheaded in Constantinople in the seventeenth century.
4-3.desc: Holy New Martyr Paul the Russian, a freed captive who was martyred in Constantinople.
4-3.name: Paul the Russian

4-3.bio:
Agape is listed in the Greek synaxaria as a virgin martyr commemorated on the third of April. Little of her life has been preserved beyond her name and her witness.

She is distinct from Agape of Thessalonica, one of the three sisters commemorated later in this month.
4-3.desc: Holy Virgin Martyr Agape, commemorated on this day in the Greek synaxaria.
4-3.name: Agape the Virgin Martyr

4-30.bio:
St. James, the son of Zebedee and elder brother of St. John the Theologian, was called by the Lord from his father's fishing boat to become one of the Twelve. With Peter and John he belonged to the innermost circle of the disciples, present at the Transfiguration and at the agony in Gethsemane.

As the Acts of the Apostles records, he was the first of the Twelve to drink the cup of martyrdom, beheaded in Jerusalem by Herod Agrippa. The Church honors him as the protomartyr among the apostles, and commemorates him on April 30.
4-30.desc: Holy Apostle James, son of Zebedee, brother of John the Theologian.
4-30.name: James the Apostle, Son of Zebedee

4-30.bio:
Donatus was Bishop of Euroea in Epirus in the fourth century, in the reign of the emperor Theodosius the Great. Tradition relates that he slew a dragon that poisoned the waters near his city, raised the dead, and brought forth a spring by his prayer.

He reposed in peace and is venerated as the patron of the region of Paramythia.
4-30.desc: Saint Donatus, Bishop of Euroea in Epirus, wonderworker.
4-30.name: Donatus of Euroea

4-30.bio:
Clement was a monk and later abbot of the Monastery of the Studion in Constantinople in the ninth century, a disciple of the tradition of Saint Theodore the Studite. He composed many canons and hymns for the feasts of the Church.

He suffered for the holy icons and reposed in peace.
4-30.desc: Venerable Clement the Hymnographer, abbot of the Studion.
4-30.name: Clement the Hymnographer

4-30.bio:
Maximus was a Christian of Ephesus who, in the persecution of the emperor Decius, presented himself before the proconsul and confessed Christ. He refused to sacrifice to the idols.

He was stoned to death in the third century.
4-30.desc: Holy Martyr Maximus of Ephesus, who suffered under Decius.
4-30.name: Maximus of Ephesus

4-30.bio:
Ignatius was born in 1807 to a noble family and, after a brilliant beginning as a military engineer, left the world for the monastic life. He became abbot of the Sergiev Hermitage near Saint Petersburg and later Bishop of the Caucasus and Stavropol.

Retiring to a monastery, he devoted his last years to writing; his works on the spiritual life, above all The Arena, remain widely read. He reposed in 1867.
4-30.desc: Saint Ignatius Brianchaninov, Bishop of the Caucasus and Stavropol, ascetic writer.
4-30.name: Ignatius Brianchaninov

4-30.bio:
Aphrodisios is commemorated in the Greek synaxaria as a hieromartyr who was put to death for Christ together with thirty companions. The details of their martyrdom have not been preserved.

The Church keeps their memory together on this day.
4-30.desc: Hieromartyr Aphrodisios and the thirty martyrs who suffered with him.
4-30.name: Aphrodisios and the Thirty Martyrs

4-4.bio:
St. Titus was a disciple and companion of the Apostle Paul, who called him his true son in the common faith. A Greek by birth, he accompanied Paul on his apostolic journeys, was entrusted with delicate missions to the churches, and received the epistle that bears his name, in which Paul instructs him in the ordering of the Church.

According to tradition Paul established him as bishop of Crete, where he shepherded the faithful to a great old age and reposed in peace, the father of the Church of that island. He is commemorated on April 4.
4-4.desc: Holy Apostle Titus, disciple of Paul.
4-4.name: Titos

4-4.bio:
St. Claudia was a martyr of the early Church who suffered for Christ during the Roman persecutions. The synaxaria preserve little of her life beyond her faithful confession, numbering her among the holy women who chose death rather than deny the Lord.

In honoring her, the Church honors the great company of women martyrs whose names are known while their full stories are written in heaven. She is commemorated on April 4.
4-4.name: Claudia

4-4.bio:
Zosimas entered the monastic life as a child and lived for many decades in a monastery of Palestine before moving to a community near the Jordan. Going into the desert during Great Lent, as was the custom there, he met the ascetic Mary of Egypt and heard from her the story of her repentance.

The following year he brought her Holy Communion, and a year later found her body and buried it. He lived to a great age and reposed in peace in the sixth century.
4-4.desc: Venerable Zosimas of Palestine, the elder who met Saint Mary of Egypt in the desert beyond the Jordan.
4-4.name: Zosimas of Palestine

4-4.bio:
Pherbutha was the sister of the hieromartyr Simeon, bishop of Persia. After his death she, her widowed sister, and her servant were accused of sorcery by the Zoroastrian priests and brought before the Persian king.

Refusing to deny Christ, they were put to death in the fourth century, tradition relating that they were sawn asunder. They are remembered among the martyrs of the great persecution under Shapur.
4-4.desc: Holy Martyr Pherbutha of Persia, with her sister and her servant.
4-4.name: Pherbutha of Persia

4-4.bio:
Publius lived as a hermit in the Egyptian desert in the fourth century. Tradition relates that by his prayers he hindered a demon sent by the emperor Julian the Apostate, who had set out to make war on the Persians.

He reposed in peace in the desert.
4-4.desc: Venerable Publius, ascetic of the Egyptian desert in the days of Julian the Apostate.
4-4.name: Publius of Egypt

4-4.bio:
Plato was born in Constantinople in the eighth century, orphaned young, and became a monk on Mount Olympus in Bithynia. He founded the Monastery of Sakkoudion and later guided his nephew Theodore, who became the great abbot of the Studion.

He suffered imprisonment and exile both for the holy icons and for opposing the unlawful marriage of the emperor. He reposed in the early ninth century at the Studion, honoured as a confessor.
4-4.desc: Venerable Plato, abbot of Sakkoudion and uncle of Saint Theodore the Studite, confessor for the icons.
4-4.name: Plato of Studion

4-4.bio:
Theonas lived on Mount Athos in the sixteenth century as a disciple of Saint James of Kastoria, and after his teacher's martyrdom founded the Monastery of Saint Anastasia Pharmakolytria near Thessalonica.

He was later chosen Archbishop of Thessalonica, where he shepherded his flock under Ottoman rule and reposed in peace. His incorrupt relics are kept in his monastery.
4-4.desc: Saint Theonas, Archbishop of Thessalonica and founder of the Monastery of Saint Anastasia.
4-4.name: Theonas of Thessalonica

4-4.bio:
George refused a marriage arranged by his parents and withdrew to Mount Maleon in the Peloponnese, where he lived as a monk in the ninth century. He was granted the gift of foresight and, tradition relates, foretold the day of his own repose.

He is one of the holy ascetics of Laconia venerated by the local faithful.
4-4.desc: Venerable George, ascetic of Mount Maleon in the Peloponnese.
4-4.name: George of Maleon

4-5.bio:
St. Theodoulos was a young reader of the church of Thessaloniki who suffered martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century. Tradition remembers him together with the elder deacon Agathopous; refusing to surrender the holy books or deny Christ, the two were condemned and cast into the sea.

The Church honors in him the courage of the young, who at the very start of life counted Christ dearer than all its promise. He is commemorated on April 5.
4-5.name: Theodoulos

4-5.bio:
