These seven martyrs are commemorated together in the Greek synaxaria. Tradition places their martyrdom at Corinth in the persecution of the third century, where after various tortures they were put to death for Christ.

They are also remembered with the martyrs of Corinth at the end of January.
4-5.desc: Holy Martyrs Claudius, Diodorus, Victor, Victorinus, Pappias, Serapion and Nicephorus, who suffered at Corinth.
4-5.greek: Κλαύδιος, Διόδωρος, Ουίκτωρ, Ουικτωρίνος, Παππίας, Σεραπίων και Νικηφόρος
4-5.name: Claudius, Diodorus, Victor, Victorinus, Pappias, Serapion and Nicephorus

4-5.bio:
Theodora, a Christian maiden of Alexandria, refused to sacrifice to idols and was condemned to a house of shame. The soldier Didymus, himself a Christian, entered in disguise, exchanged clothes with her and let her escape.

When the deception was discovered Didymus was sentenced to death, and Theodora came forward to share his fate. Both were beheaded at the beginning of the fourth century.
4-5.desc: Holy Martyrs Theodora the Virgin and Didymus the Soldier of Alexandria.
4-5.name: Theodora and Didymus of Alexandria

4-5.bio:
Argyre was born in Prousa in Bithynia and was married young. A Turkish neighbour who desired her, and was refused, accused her falsely of having promised to embrace Islam, and she was brought to trial.

She steadfastly confessed Christ and was imprisoned in Constantinople, where after many years of hardship she died in her chains in the eighteenth century. Her relics were later found incorrupt and are venerated by the faithful.
4-5.desc: Holy New Martyr Argyre of Prousa, who died in prison in Constantinople for refusing to deny Christ.
4-5.name: Argyre the New Martyr

4-5.bio:
Theodora was born on the island of Aegina in the ninth century and married there; fleeing Arab raids, the family settled in Thessalonica. After the death of her husband she entered the convent of Saint Stephen in that city, where her own daughter later became abbess.

She lived in great humility and obedience for many years and reposed in peace. Her relics were found fragrant and myrrh-streaming and have worked many healings.
4-5.desc: Venerable Theodora of Thessalonica, nun and wonderworker whose relics streamed myrrh.
4-5.name: Theodora of Thessalonica

4-5.bio:
George was a Christian of Ephesus in Asia Minor who, in the years of Ottoman rule, was pressed to abandon his faith. Tradition relates that he confessed Christ firmly before the authorities and was put to death in his native region in the early nineteenth century.

He is one of the many new martyrs of Asia Minor honoured by the Greek Church.
4-5.desc: Holy New Martyr George of Ephesus, who suffered under Ottoman rule.
4-5.name: George of Ephesus

4-5.bio:
Panagiotis was a young Christian who, according to the synaxaria, was slandered before the Ottoman authorities in Jerusalem and pressed to renounce his faith. He refused to deny Christ and was beheaded in the Holy City in the early nineteenth century.

He is numbered among the new martyrs of the Ottoman period.
4-5.desc: Holy New Martyr Panagiotis, who was martyred in Jerusalem.
4-5.name: Panagiotis of Jerusalem

4-6.bio:
St. Eutychios was Patriarch of Constantinople in the sixth century, in the days of the emperor Justinian. A monk raised to the patriarchal throne, he presided at the Fifth Ecumenical Council, and later, refusing to accept a teaching that compromised the reality of Christ's human nature, he was deposed and spent years in exile in a monastery.

Restored at last to his throne, he ended his days in peace, honored as a confessor for the truth of the Incarnation. He is commemorated on April 6.
4-6.name: Eutychios

4-6.bio:
Gregory was born in Asia Minor in the thirteenth century, was taken captive by the Turks, and after his ransom became a monk on Sinai, then in Crete, and finally on Mount Athos. There he taught the practice of inner stillness and the Jesus Prayer, gathering many disciples.

Driven from Athos by Turkish raids, he settled at Paroria on the Bulgarian border, where his community became a fountain of hesychasm for the Slavic lands. He reposed in the fourteenth century.
4-6.desc: Venerable Gregory of Sinai, hesychast father and teacher of the prayer of the heart.
4-6.name: Gregory of Sinai

4-6.bio:
Platonis served as a deaconess and then withdrew to the desert near Nisibis in Mesopotamia, where she founded a community of nuns under a strict rule of prayer, fasting and silence.

She guided her sisters by her own example and reposed in peace in the early fourth century.
4-6.desc: Venerable Platonis, deaconess and foundress of a women's monastery near Nisibis.
4-6.name: Platonis of Nisibis

4-6.bio:
These one hundred and twenty Christians were captured in the wars between the Byzantine and Persian empires in the fourth century and held in Persia. When they refused to worship fire and the sun they were condemned.

Tradition relates that they were burned alive together after firmly confessing their faith.
4-6.desc: The Holy 120 Martyrs who were burned for Christ in Persia.
4-6.name: 120 Martyrs of Persia

4-6.bio:
Gennadios was a monk of the Dionysiou Monastery on Mount Athos. Tradition relates that as a youth he had been pressed to accept Islam and, repenting, went to Constantinople to confess Christ openly.

He was beheaded there in the early nineteenth century and is honoured among the Athonite new martyrs.
4-6.desc: Holy New Martyr Gennadios of the Monastery of Dionysiou on Mount Athos.
4-6.name: Gennadios of Dionysiou

4-6.bio:
Gregory came from Constantinople to Mount Athos in the fourteenth century and lived in stillness in the desert places of the Holy Mountain. He is remembered chiefly as the elder who guided the young Gregory Palamas in the life of prayer.

He reposed in peace on Athos.
4-6.desc: Venerable Gregory the Byzantine, Athonite hesychast and spiritual teacher of Saint Gregory Palamas.
4-6.name: Gregory the Byzantine

4-6.bio:
These five Christians of Samothrace had, under duress after the island was ravaged by the Turks, outwardly accepted Islam. Repenting, they returned openly to the Christian faith.

They were seized and put to death at Makri in Thrace in 1835, and are honoured together by the Church.
4-6.desc: Holy New Martyrs George, Manuel, Theodore, George and Michael of Samothrace.
4-6.name: Five New Martyrs of Samothrace

4-7.bio:
St. George the Confessor was Bishop of Mytilene on the island of Lesbos during the age of iconoclasm. A merciful shepherd known for his almsgiving and ascetic life, he refused to abandon the veneration of the holy icons when the emperors demanded it, and in his old age he was driven from his see into exile, where he ended his days.

The faithful of Lesbos have honored him from ancient times among their chief intercessors. He is commemorated on April 7.
4-7.desc: St. George the Confessor, Bishop of Mytilene.
4-7.name: George of Mytilene

4-7.bio:
Kalliopios was born in Perge in Pamphylia to a devout widow named Theoklia, who raised him in the faith. During the persecution of the early fourth century he confessed Christ at Pompeiopolis in Cilicia and was cruelly tortured.

Tradition relates that he was crucified head downward during Holy Week, and that his mother received his body and buried it.
4-7.desc: Holy Martyr Kalliopios of Perge, crucified for Christ at Pompeiopolis in Cilicia.
4-7.name: Kalliopios the Martyr

4-7.bio:
Rufinus, a deacon, and Aquilina were imprisoned at Sinope on the Black Sea for their faith. Tradition relates that through their prayers and miracles two hundred soldiers of the garrison came to believe in Christ.

All were beheaded together in the persecution of the early fourth century.
4-7.desc: Holy Martyrs Rufinus the Deacon, Aquilina and two hundred soldiers who believed through them, at Sinope.
4-7.greek: Ρουφίνος, Ακυλίνα και οι Διακόσιοι Μάρτυρες
4-7.name: Rufinus, Aquilina and the 200 Soldiers of Sinope

4-7.bio:
Tikhon was born Vasily Belavin in 1865, the son of a village priest. As a young bishop he headed the Russian mission in North America, founding parishes and seminaries across the continent, before returning to serve as bishop in Yaroslavl and Vilnius.

In 1917 he was elected Patriarch of Moscow, the first in two centuries, and led the Church through the first years of Bolshevik persecution, enduring house arrest and constant pressure. He reposed in 1925 and was glorified as a confessor.
4-7.desc: Saint Tikhon, Patriarch of Moscow and All Russia, confessor and enlightener of North America.
4-7.name: Tikhon of Moscow

4-7.bio:
Gerasimos came from Constantinople to Mount Athos, where he lived the ascetic life and composed hymns and services for the saints. He is remembered as a man of learning and prayer.

He reposed in peace on the Holy Mountain in the eighteenth century.
4-7.desc: Venerable Gerasimos the Byzantine, Athonite ascetic and hymnographer.
4-7.name: Gerasimos the Byzantine

4-7.bio:
Daniel was born in Pereslavl-Zalessky in the fifteenth century and became a monk at the Borovsk monastery under a disciple of Saint Paphnutius. Returning to his native town, he made it his special labour to bury the unclaimed dead and to pray for them.

On the burial ground he founded the Trinity Monastery, of which he became abbot. He reposed in the sixteenth century and is venerated as a wonderworker.
4-7.desc: Venerable Daniel, abbot of Pereslavl-Zalessky and founder of the Trinity Monastery there.
4-7.name: Daniel of Pereslavl

4-8.bio:
St. Kalliope is honored among the martyrs of the early Church, one of those who suffered for Christ during the Roman persecutions. The synaxaria preserve little of her life beyond her faithful confession unto death.

Her name, which in Greek means beautiful voice, has been borne by generations of faithful women in her honor, and the Church keeps her memory among the victorious martyrs. She is commemorated on April 8.
4-8.name: Kalliope

4-8.bio:
These four are numbered among the Seventy Apostles. Agabus is the prophet of the Acts of the Apostles who foretold the famine under Claudius and the arrest of Paul in Jerusalem. Rufus, greeted by Paul in the Epistle to the Romans, is said by tradition to have become bishop of Thebes in Greece.

Phlegon and Asyncritus, also greeted in the same epistle, preached the Gospel and, tradition relates, served as bishops in Marathon and in Hyrcania respectively.
4-8.desc: Holy Apostles Agabus, Rufus, Phlegon and Asyncritus of the Seventy.
4-8.name: Agabus, Rufus, Phlegon and Asyncritus

4-8.bio:
Celestine was Bishop of Rome from 422 to 432. Learned in the Scriptures, he was a firm defender of the Orthodox faith and condemned the teaching of Nestorius, sending his legates to the Third Ecumenical Council at Ephesus.

He reposed in peace and is honoured by the Eastern Church among the holy popes of old Rome.
4-8.desc: Saint Celestine, Pope of Rome, champion of Orthodoxy against Nestorius.
4-8.name: Celestine of Rome

4-8.bio:
Pausilypos confessed Christ at Heraclea in Thrace during the reign of the emperor Hadrian in the second century. He was scourged with iron rods and handed over for further torment.

Tradition relates that he escaped his bonds but died soon afterward of his wounds, receiving the martyr's crown.
4-8.desc: Holy Martyr Pausilypos, who suffered at Heraclea in Thrace under Hadrian.
4-8.name: Pausilypos of Heraclea

4-8.bio:
John was a ship-owner of the island of Kos who, tradition relates, was falsely accused of having accepted Islam and was pressed to confirm it. He firmly confessed that he was a Christian and would die as one.

He was burned alive on Kos in the seventeenth century and is honoured among the new martyrs of the Dodecanese.
4-8.desc: Holy New Martyr John the Ship-Captain of Kos, burned for Christ.
4-8.name: John the Ship-Captain

4-8.bio:
Niphon was a monk of the Kiev Caves Monastery, chosen Bishop of Novgorod in the twelfth century. He was a strict ascetic and a builder of churches, and defended the canonical order of the Church in a time of political strife.

He reposed at the Kiev Caves and was buried there.
4-8.desc: Saint Niphon, Bishop of Novgorod, monk of the Kiev Caves.
4-8.name: Niphon of Novgorod

4-8.bio:
John Koulikas was a Christian who, in the sixteenth century, was accused before the Ottoman authorities and urged to embrace Islam. He refused and confessed Christ.

Tradition relates that he was impaled and so received the crown of martyrdom.
4-8.desc: Holy New Martyr John Koulikas, who was impaled for Christ.
4-8.name: John Koulikas

4-9.bio:
St. Eudemos is remembered among the martyrs of the early Church, one who confessed Christ in the time of the persecutions and sealed his faith with suffering. The synaxaria preserve little of his life beyond this faithful witness.

The Church honors in him and in the countless martyrs like him the cloud of witnesses whose endurance watered the seed of the Gospel. He is commemorated on April 9.
4-9.name: Eudemos

4-9.bio:
Raphael, an archimandrite, and his deacon Nicholas were living at the monastery of Karyes near Thermi on Lesbos when the Turks attacked in 1463, ten years after the fall of Constantinople. With them was the twelve-year-old Irene, daughter of the village elder, and others who had taken refuge there.

All were cruelly put to death on Bright Tuesday. Their story was forgotten until 1959, when the saints appeared in dreams to many villagers and their relics were uncovered; they are now among the most beloved saints of Greece and are also honoured on Bright Tuesday each year.
4-9.desc: Holy New Martyrs Raphael, Nicholas and Irene of Lesbos, martyred at Thermi and revealed five centuries later.
4-9.name: Raphael, Nicholas and Irene of Lesbos

4-9.bio:
Eupsychios was a young Christian of Caesarea in Cappadocia, newly married, when the emperor Julian the Apostate sought to restore pagan worship. With other Christians he took part in the destruction of a pagan temple in the city.

He was arrested, tortured, and beheaded in the fourth century, and Saint Basil the Great later honoured his memory.
4-9.desc: Holy Martyr Eupsychios of Caesarea in Cappadocia, who suffered under Julian the Apostate.
4-9.name: Eupsychios of Caesarea

4-9.bio:
Bademus was born to a wealthy family in Persia and, giving away his possessions, founded a monastery near Bethlapat, gathering disciples around him. In the persecution of King Shapur he was imprisoned with seven of his monks.

Tradition relates that a Christian nobleman who had apostatized was ordered to kill him, and struck him many blows before he died. He is honoured among the martyrs of Persia of the fourth century.
4-9.desc: Holy Monk-Martyr Bademus, archimandrite in Persia, with seven of his disciples.
4-9.name: Bademus of Persia

4-9.bio:
Abdiesus was among a great company of Christians, clergy and laity, taken captive in the Persian wars and held in Persia during the persecution of King Shapur. When they refused to worship the sun they were put to death together.

Tradition numbers the company at more than two hundred and seventy, including a bishop and priests.
4-9.desc: Holy Martyrs Abdiesus and those with him, who suffered in Persia under Shapur.
4-9.name: Abdiesus and the Martyrs of Persia

4-9.bio:
Acacius was Bishop of Amida in Mesopotamia in the fifth century. When thousands of Persian prisoners of war were dying of hunger, he sold the gold and silver vessels of his church to feed them and send them home.

Tradition relates that the Persian king, moved by this charity, sought peace with the Romans. Acacius reposed in peace.
4-9.desc: Saint Acacius, Bishop of Amida, who sold the church's vessels to ransom Persian captives.
4-9.name: Acacius of Amida
